headline: New moon springs load the Moriches cut as fluke push out and the first bonito show at the bar
subhead: Warm bay water is shoving fluke toward the inlet channels while building tides set up a real outgoing bite through the weekend.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what warm bay water does in early July — it got soft and slow on the flats and pushed everything with fins toward moving water. Great South Bay readings crossed 78.8°F, and while I don't have a thermometer sitting in the Moriches system itself, the same signature showed up here: fluke that were spread thin over Pattersquash flats and the East Moriches grass beds a week ago are now stacking against hard structure — the inlet's main channel edge, the Cupsogue drop-off, and the deeper cuts along Tuthill Point. Warm, oxygen-poor shallow water pushes bait and predators alike into anything with current and depth, and the inlet is the biggest current-and-depth feature we've got. That's the whole story behind this week's pattern.

We're building toward a new moon, with the tidal springs stacking hard through the weekend — peak alignment looks to land July 11-13. That matters more here than almost anywhere on the South Shore because Moriches Inlet is a narrow, engineered-by-nature cut with a shifting bar, and bigger tidal exchange means more velocity through that throat. More velocity means more bait getting flushed out of the bay on the outgoing, which means predators — bass, blues, fluke — stack on the downcurrent side of the bar and the eastern rock jetty waiting on it. If you've fished this inlet long enough you know the drill: neap tides let fish spread out and sulk in eddies, spring tides concentrate everything into predictable lanes. This is a spring-tide week. Fish the lanes.

Fluke first, because that's where the volume is right now. The drift along the main channel edge off Pattersquash Island, running 18 to 25 feet, has been the most consistent water in the system. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 1- to 1.5-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the outgoing, have been putting keeper fluke in the boat — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 21 inches with the occasional better fish mixed in, which tracks with what's being reported from Shinnecock and the Reynolds Channel side too. The other lane worth working is the deeper hole just inside the inlet proper, on the bay side of the current bar position — that hole has held its depth through this spring's storm cycles and it's collecting fish getting pushed off the flats. Don't waste time on the shallow grass flats behind Cupsogue right now; the water's too warm and the fluke have already voted with their fins.

Striped bass are doing what they do at this inlet in summer — showing best on the edges of light, not the middle of the day. The outgoing tide at dusk, worked with bunker chunks on a fishfinder rig tight to the rocks on the ocean side of the Cupsogue jetty, has produced keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of shorts. If you want numbers over size, work the surf at first light with topwater plugs or bucktail-and-swim-shad combos along the ocean bar east of the inlet mouth — that structure has been holding schoolies stacked tight, and a few 28- to 32-inch fish have come out of that same stretch on outgoing water. The bigger springs building this weekend should sharpen that bite further; more water moving through the cut means a harder edge for bass to sit on.

Bluefish are around in the usual two flavors — snapper blues thick in the bay proper, especially off the Forge River mouth and up into East Moriches creeks, and better cocktail-to-medium blues showing at the inlet itself on diamond jigs and small metal worked on the outgoing tide alongside the fluke and bass. If you're throwing bucktails for fluke and getting your leader bit off, that's not bad luck, that's just Tuesday at this inlet in July.

Honest note on weakfish: water's warm enough on paper, but I'm not hearing anything real out of this system, and that lines up with what the broader region is showing — warm water alone hasn't been translating to weakfish activity anywhere close by this year. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. Porgies are a better bet if you want a bend in the rod without overthinking it — sandworms and clam on standard rigs over the deeper holes off Tuthill Point have been steady, if unspectacular.

The one genuinely new development is on the ocean side. This is the tail end of the seasonal window for the first bonito and Spanish mackerel showing at eastern Long Island inlets, and Moriches and Shinnecock have both had early reports on clean incoming water at the ocean bar. If you've got small metal — deadly dicks, epoxy jigs, anything that moves fast and flashes — it's worth a half hour at the bar on a clean incoming tide before you commit to the fluke drift. That window closes fast; by next week the bulk of that bite typically slides east.

Look-ahead: with the new moon springs peaking Friday through Monday, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet channel edge for fluke, and hit the ocean bar at first light for bass and a shot at bonito before the sun gets up. If the bar's still shifted where it was after the spring storm cycle, expect the strongest current lane to be tighter to the Cupsogue side than the Pattersquash side — that's where I'd start the drift.
